title: Target Sum
statement: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, put a '+' or a '-' in front of every number and concatenate them into an expression. Return how many different assignments of signs produce an expression that evaluates to the target.
realWorld: Balancing a ledger: given a set of amounts that must each be credited or debited, count the ways the two sides can differ by a required figure. The same reduction turns any 'assign each item to one of two groups' question — two-machine load balancing, splitting a batch across two regions — into a subset-sum.

examples.explanation: Four plus signs and one minus: 5 - 1 - 1 = 3, and the minus can sit on any of the five ones. Equivalently, choose which four numbers are positive: C(5,4) = 5.
The total is 10, so the positive group would have to sum to (10 + 5) / 2 = 7.5. No integer subset exists, and the parity check catches this before any searching happens.
+1+0-1, +1-0-1, -1+0+1, -1-0+1. A zero can carry either sign without changing the value, so every zero doubles the count — an easy case to get wrong.

constraints: Zeros are allowed and each one doubles the number of assignments

bruteForce.whySlow: Two branches per number gives 2^n leaves — a million for twenty numbers, and every one of them is expanded to full depth before the comparison happens. The repetition is easy to name: the state that matters at index i is only the running total, yet with twenty small numbers there are a few thousand reachable totals and a million paths reaching them, so 'the number of ways to finish from index 10 with a running total of 7' is recomputed hundreds of times and returns the same value every time.

patternIdentification: Every element gets one of two symmetric labels and the question is about the resulting totals — that is the signal to stop searching over sign assignments and solve for the groups algebraically. Call P the sum of the numbers given a plus and N the sum of the rest. Then P + N = total and P - N = target, so P = (total + target) / 2, and counting sign assignments becomes counting subsets that sum to P: plain 0/1 subset-sum. The algebra also hands you two free rejections that no search would find on its own — if total + target is odd then P is not an integer, and if |target| > total then P is out of range, so the answer is 0 before any work is done. From there the state is dp[s] = the number of subsets of the numbers seen so far that sum to exactly s, the recurrence per number is dp[s] += dp[s - num], and the base case is dp[0] = 1 because exactly one subset (the empty one) sums to zero. Partition Equal Subset Sum is the same machine with 'count' swapped for 'is it reachable'.

optimized.idea: Reduce to subset-sum with capacity (total + target) / 2, guarding parity and range first. Then run the counting knapsack over a single array: for each number, sweep the capacity axis downwards so that dp[s - num] still describes the state before this number was offered, which is what keeps each number from being used twice.

commonMistakes: Skipping the parity check and letting Java's integer division round (total + target) / 2 down. The code then confidently solves a different problem: [1,2,7] with target 5 gives capacity 7, finds the subset {7}, and returns 1 where the answer is 0.

Omitting the |target| > total guard. When target is below -total the capacity comes out negative and new int[capacity + 1] throws NegativeArraySizeException — nums = [1] with target = -100 crashes rather than returning 0.

Sweeping the capacity axis upwards (for s = num; s <= capacity; s++). dp[s - num] has already been updated for this same number, so numbers get reused and the count is inflated: [1,1,1,1,1] with target 3 returns far more than 5, while small inputs with distinct values can still look correct.
